editorial.heading: Why this one exists
editorial.body: The Weekender is the bag Asekho built for himself first, in 1999, out of an offcut nobody else wanted. It has been redrawn four times since. The proportions have not changed: wide enough for three days, narrow enough to sit at your feet on a bus to Mthatha.

editorial.heading: The quill
editorial.body: Full-quill means the panels come from the prime back of the bird, where the follicles stand proud. We cut so the quill field runs unbroken across the front — which costs hide, and is the whole point. No two fronts match. Yours will be read at a glance across a room.

editorial.heading: How it ages
editorial.body: Ostrich takes on a soft sheen where your hand falls. The lining darkens first, then the corners, then the base. Twenty-seven years of these bags coming back for repair has taught us that people do not want them to look new. They want them to look theirs.

editorial.heading: The hide chooses the bag
editorial.body: Nguni cattle carry their own map — every hide is patterned differently, and we cut to the pattern rather than against it. You are not choosing a colourway. You are choosing an animal, and we will send you a photograph of the actual hide before we cut it.

editorial.heading: Built for the road, not the shelf
editorial.body: Named for the street the first workshop sat on. Short handles, wide mouth, a base that takes a knock. It is the bag people buy when they have already ruined two nylon ones.

products.priceNote: Price includes VAT and delivery anywhere in South Africa.
products.materialLine: Nile crocodile belly, CITES-documented. Full-grain interior. Solid brass locks.
products.moodLine: It does not announce itself. It does not need to.

images.alt: The Sovereign Attaché in Nile crocodile belly leather, front view
Close detail of the crocodile belly scale pattern across the front panel
The Attaché open, showing the padded fourteen-inch laptop sleeve

personalisation.label: Brass shank, stamped with your initials

editorial.heading: Belly, centred
editorial.body: Crocodile is judged on the belly — the small, even scales down the centre line. We centre that line on the front panel and let it run out to the sides, which means the two halves of the bag are cut from opposite ends of the same skin. It is the most expensive way to lay a pattern and the only one worth doing.

editorial.heading: Papers included
editorial.body: Every crocodile piece leaves the workshop with its CITES documentation. Keep it with the bag. It travels with you, and it is what separates a legitimate skin from a story.

editorial.heading: A working bag
editorial.body: Fourteen-inch laptop, a folder of paper, a charger, and nothing rattling. The lid closes flat because the gussets are cut, not gathered. It stands up on its own when you put it down.
